idiom_name: Ktorm Entity interface + bound Table + flushChanges (Exposed DAO as the alternative)
implementation_notes: Kotlin's ORMs express the pattern without a base class: in Ktorm the entity is an interface extending Entity<E>, instantiated through Entity.create/Entity.Factory with a JDK dynamic proxy that tracks property changes, while the table object declares the mapping with bindTo/references and the entity's changes are written with flushChanges. Exposed's DAO API is the equivalent second library (Entity.newEntity, entity.flush()); what replaces the classic superclass-and-reflection structure is a pair of declarations - entity interface plus Table object - so the mapping sits visibly on the table side instead of being inferred. The classic form remains sensible while each entity is one table; entities as interfaces (not data classes) are the price Ktorm charges for proxy-based change tracking.
pitfalls: Entities are proxies, so equality, hashCode and toString are not data-class semantics; do not rely on structural equality in collections.
A property that was never set has no value at all: flushChanges writes nothing for it and reading it returns a type default ("" or 0), which can mask bugs that a nullable type would have caught.
Change tracking lives in the proxy: serialising and re-creating an entity (caches, HTTP) loses that state, so the flushed object must be the same instance the framework handed you.
